title: John Prepares the Way, and the Son Is Named
summary: In a year carefully dated by the rulers of the day, the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. He calls Israel to a baptism of repentance, tells ordinary people what fruit that repentance should bear, and points to a coming one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, before Herod silences him in prison. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends, the Father's voice names him beloved Son, and Luke traces his line all the way back to Adam and to God.
story: Luke's first two chapters told of two births, John's and Jesus', and ended with the boy Jesus in the temple. Now roughly eighteen years pass in silence and both sons are grown. The prophetic voice that fell quiet in Israel returns with John, and his work is to get a people ready. Then the story turns to Jesus: at his baptism heaven itself declares who he is, and the genealogy that follows sets that declaration inside the whole human story. With this chapter the public ministry is about to begin, and the next scene, the temptation in the wilderness, will test the title the Father has just spoken.
historical:
Luke dates John's call the way ancient historians dated events, by the officeholders of the year. Tiberius became emperor after Augustus died in AD 14, so his fifteenth year falls around AD 28 or 29; some reckon from an earlier shared rule with Augustus and arrive at about AD 26 or 27. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36. After Herod the Great died in 4 BC his kingdom was divided among his sons: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch (a ruler of part of a divided territory, lower than a king), and Philip ruled the lands northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Lysanias of Abilene, north of Damascus, is less known; an older Lysanias died decades earlier, and an inscription from Abila is usually read as referring to a later tetrarch of that name. Annas had been high priest from AD 6 until he was removed about AD 15, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36. Luke names both because Annas remained the power behind the office.

The Jewish historian Josephus, writing near the end of the first century, also tells of John the Baptist, describes him as a good man who urged righteousness and baptism, and reports that Antipas imprisoned and executed him, fearing his influence with the crowds. Luke gives the moral reason: John rebuked Antipas for taking Herodias, the wife of his half-brother, which the Law of Moses forbade (Leviticus 18:16).
cultural:
Ritual washing was common in Judaism of the Second Temple period (the era from the rebuilding of the temple in the late sixth century BC to its destruction in AD 70); stepped immersion pools have been found near the temple and in the houses of priests, and the community at Qumran by the Dead Sea practiced repeated washings. John's baptism was different: it was a single act, done by him, tied to repentance and forgiveness, and offered to Jews, who normally did not think they needed the kind of entry rite later given to converts. His warning, “We have Abraham as our father”, strikes at the belief that descent from Abraham guaranteed a place among God's people.

The people who ask, “What then should we do?”, are concrete figures. Tax collectors bid for the right to collect tolls and customs and made their living on the surplus, which made them despised as extortioners and collaborators. The soldiers were probably troops serving Antipas or other local authorities rather than Roman legionaries. Carrying a master's sandals or untying their straps was a slave's task, so John places himself lower than a slave before the coming one. A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind so the heavy wheat fell and the chaff blew aside to be burned.
literary: The chapter opens like a prophetic book: “the word of God came to John”, much as it came to Jeremiah or Hosea. Luke quotes Isaiah 40:3-5 at greater length than Matthew 3 or Mark 1, carrying it through to “all humanity will see God’s salvation” because that universal note runs through his whole work. John's preaching comes in three parts: warning (7-9), practical instruction unique to Luke (10-14), and messianic promise (15-17). Luke then reports John's imprisonment (19-20) before the baptism, clearing the stage for Jesus even though the arrest happened later. The genealogy runs backward, son of, son of, son of, and ends with “the son of Adam, the son of God,” echoing the voice at the baptism.

outline.t: The word of God comes to John in the wilderness
Warning to the crowds: bear fruit
What repentance looks like for crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers
The one more powerful who is coming
The genealogy of Jesus from Joseph to Adam

doctrines.note: Repentance in this chapter is a turning that shows up in behavior: sharing clothing and food, honest collection, no extortion. John refuses to let ancestry or religious identity replace it.

At the baptism the Son prays, the Spirit descends in bodily form, and the Father speaks from heaven. The church has long read the scene as one of the clearest pictures of the three persons of the one God acting together.
John speaks of coming wrath, an axe at the root, and chaff burned in unquenchable fire. The good news he proclaims (verse 18) includes this warning, because the coming one will sort his harvest.

words.note: Metanoia, repentance. The word literally suggests a change of mind, but in the Greek Bible and in John's preaching it carries the Hebrew idea of turning back to God. Luke insists it has fruit, visible changes in how people handle money, power, and possessions.

Baptizo, to dip or immerse. It could describe washing as well as plunging. John uses the same verb for his own water baptism and for the coming one's baptism with the Holy Spirit and fire, which Luke will show poured out at Pentecost in Acts 2.

Agapetos, beloved. Often used of an only or specially cherished child. The Father's words at the baptism echo Psalm 2:7, where God addresses his anointed king as son, and Isaiah 42:1, where God delights in his chosen servant.

christ: The chapter shows who Jesus is by two witnesses. John, the greatest prophet of his time, says he is not worthy to untie the straps of this man's sandals, and that the coming one will do what no prophet could: pour out God's own Spirit. Then heaven speaks: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.” Luke notes that Jesus was praying when this happened, the first of many moments where he shows Jesus at prayer. By joining the crowds in a baptism of repentance, the sinless Son stands with sinners from the first day of his ministry. The genealogy extends that solidarity to everyone: Luke traces Jesus not only to David and Abraham, as Matthew does, but to Adam, so that he belongs to the whole human family, the true Son who will succeed where Adam failed.

hard.q: Why do Luke's and Matthew's genealogies of Jesus disagree?
hard.a:
The two lists agree from Abraham to David but then divide. Matthew traces the line through Solomon and the kings of Judah and names Jacob as Joseph's father; Luke traces it through another son of David, Nathan, and names Heli. The two lists meet briefly at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel and then part again. Luke also includes a Cainan (verse 36) who appears in the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament, but not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11.

Three main explanations have been offered. One holds that Luke gives Mary's line: Heli was Mary's father, and Joseph is called his son as a son-in-law, which fits Luke's wording that Jesus was regarded as Joseph's son. A second, recorded in the early third century by Julius Africanus, holds that both lists are Joseph's: one gives the legal line and the other the natural line, joined by a levirate marriage in which a man raised children in the name of his dead brother. A third, common among critical scholars, holds that the two evangelists drew on different traditions and shaped them for theological ends (Matthew's royal line in groups of fourteen, Luke's universal line reaching to Adam) and that they cannot be fully harmonized. Each view has defenders who take Scripture seriously. What both genealogies plainly affirm is that Jesus comes from David's house and from Abraham's family, and Luke adds that he belongs to all humanity.

questions: John's answers to the crowds, the tax collectors, and the soldiers are specific to their situations. What would his answer be to someone in your work or position?
What kinds of inherited identity (family, church, nation) do people rely on today the way John's hearers relied on having Abraham as their father?
Jesus begins his ministry by standing in line with sinners at the river. What does that tell you about how he approaches people?
